articles.title: Tributes paid to 'Mirfield's finest' actor Sir Patrick Stewart
articles.summary: Tributes have been paid to the legendary Star Trek actor Sir Patrick Stewart, who was born in Mirfield.
articles.body:
The Mirfield-born actor, best known for his roles in Star Trek and the X-Men films, died at the age of 86 at his home in Los Angeles on Wednesday after suffering with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia.

His death has prompted an outpouring of love from the community he proudly called home, along with his beloved Huddersfield Town - the club he followed from childhood.

Stewart's friend and fellow legendary actor Sir Ian McKellen said Stewart "never forsook his origins".

He added: "Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end."

Referencing a trait often associated with people from the region McKellen said Stewart "told you what he thought and felt".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "very sad" to hear about Stewart's death, describing him as "one of the very best" who "never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots".

In a TV interview with fellow Yorkshireman Michael Parkinson, Stewart said "we did toy" with using his regional accent when playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the Star Trek franchise.

But he added: "It was incomprehensible to the producers."

In 2004 he became chancellor of the University of Huddersfield - a role he filled until 2015. A year later the university's drama building was named after him.

Speaking at the time, he said: "I'm thrilled. It still makes me a little self conscious to think there's a building named after me."

Bob Cryan, the Vice Chancellor of the university, said Stewart was "very proud" of being chancellor and his success never changed him.

"It's something he took very personally," he said.

"He saw it as a way of paying back to Yorkshire because he was very proud of the fact that he was given a scholarship from what was then the West Riding of Yorkshire, but he felt he had never paid back."

Born in Mirfield in 1940, Stewart attended Crowlees Church of England Junior and Infant School before moving onto Mirfield Secondary Modern School.

His mother Gladys was a textile worker. She was active in amateur dramatics and encouraged her three sons to take part.

His father was a former Sergeant Major in the Parachute Regiment, whose experience during the wartime evacuation of Dunkirk had badly affected his mental health.

Stewart's love of drama came at school when one of his teachers introduced him to Shakespeare and encouraged him to perform.

His first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.

He left school at 15 and eventually got a job as a reporter and obituary writer on the Dewsbury Reporter.

He later won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School launching a career that would take him from Yorkshire to the world stage.

Although he became one of Britain's most celebrated actors through roles including in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film series, Stewart spoke of his pride in being from West Yorkshire.

Spen Valley MP Kim Leadbeater described Stewart as "Mirfield's finest".

Posting on X, the Labour MP described him as "an outstanding talent and someone who came across as a thoroughly decent and lovely".

Leadbeater said she had met the actor at Huddersfield Town football matches and corresponded with him several times, adding: "He was incredibly kind and he will be greatly missed."

A lifelong Huddersfield Town supporter, Stewart attended games when his schedule allowed and celebrated the Terriers' promotion to the Premier League at Wembley in 2017.

The club's chief operating officer David Threlfall-Sykes said: "Obviously it was Sir Patrick Stewart walking around so people would get star-struck, but he would get star-struck by seeing the players and the manager because they were his heroes.

"It was a weird dichotomy but it just shows how much this place meant to him, just like it does to everyone that comes here every weekend to fill the ground. He was no different in that respect."

For many, it was the combination of worldwide fame and his down-to-earth Yorkshire roots that made him such a star across the world.

Reflecting on his sense of humour, Cryan, of the University of Huddersfield, said: "He had a great sense of fun.

"I remember saying to him we were hosting a dinner for staff at the university to say thank you for all their hard work and we decided he and I were going to be waiters.

"You can imagine peoples' faces when Patrick served them their meal."

The statement announcing Stewart's death, which was shared on his Instagram account, ended with a quote from his memoirs: "Like me, Jean-Luc has lived an unusual life that has taken him far beyond the bounds of normal human experience.

"But he is also someone who remains true to his earthbound roots, for they are what gave him his identity. In the end, he feels the call of home, as do I."

articles.title: From green card to fraud: Kenyans arrested in $130m US ghost student scam
articles.summary: The alleged scheme used stolen identities to claim US student aid, with Kenyans among those charged.
articles.body:
In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.

Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.

On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.

Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.

Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.

The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (£15,000), according to prosecutors.

Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.

Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial. He has not yet commented on the allegations against him.

His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid that resulted in a loss of $130m in taxpayers funds.

US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments that involved Kenyan nationals, while a further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.

The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.

At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved.

"If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.

The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue.

"The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.

But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.

People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college.

"His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.

He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.

The scale of the suspected fraud is significant.

Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.

The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses.

"In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.

The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya.

In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.

With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya.

The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.

In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totalling approximately $1.44m. At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.

Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m in federal student aid.

Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.

If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.

Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.

articles.title: Eight next-generation corvettes for Indian Navy: Why this Rs 40,000-crore project is important
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Strengthening its maritime surveillance and coastal defence capabilities, the Indian Navy is set to induct eight Next Generation Corvettes
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Strengthening its maritime surveillance and coastal defence capabilities, the Indian Navy is set to induct eight Next Generation Corvettes (NGCs) under a project worth over Rs 40,000 crore cleared by the Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS), chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.The contracts for the warships are expected to be signed in the coming days with Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers (GRSE), Kolkata, and Goa Shipyard Limited, top government officials told ANI.The Navy is expected to receive the first of the eight warships by 2030, although the shipyards are exploring ways to accelerate construction and advance delivery timelines.The corvettes, weighing around 2,000 tonnes and capable of speeds of nearly 30 knots, will be designed for a range of maritime operations, including surveillance missions, escort operations, deterrence, Surface Action Group (SAG) operations, search and attack missions, and coastal defence.The addition of these versatile warships is expected to enhance the Navy's ability to monitor maritime areas, respond to emerging threats and protect India's interests at sea. Their multiple operational roles will allow the Navy to deploy them across different maritime security requirements.The project is also significant for its focus on indigenous warship design. According to the Defence Ministry, the NGCs will be built using a new in-house design developed by the Indian Navy and incorporating the latest shipbuilding technologies.The project is expected to strengthen domestic warship-building capabilities and contribute to the government's SAGAR (Security and Growth for All in the Region) initiative.

articles.title: US eyewear retailer accused of sharing customers’ prescription details and eye-exam activity with Meta as appeals court revives privacy lawsuit
articles.summary: A US eyewear retailer faces a revived privacy lawsuit after a federal appeals court reversed the dismissal of claims that it shared customers’
articles.body: A US eyewear retailer faces a revived privacy lawsuit after a federal appeals court reversed the dismissal of claims that it shared customers’ health-related information with Meta. In Rand v. Eyemart Express, five Facebook users allege that a Meta Pixel tracking tool on the retailer’s website transmitted information about their prescription-eyewear searches, prescription details and eye-exam scheduling activity to Meta without their consent. A Texas federal court dismissed the case with prejudice, but on October 23, 2026, the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed that decision and remanded the case for further proceedings. The court held that the customers had standing and had adequately alleged that their health information was shared with Meta, sending the case back to the district court to reconsider their claims. The ruling does not determine whether Eyemart Express violated any law. The court noted that the parties cited, and it knew of, no earlier circuit ruling on Pixel tracking of health information specifically.Eyemart Express Meta Pixel lawsuit: what customers allege about prescription data, eye exams and Facebook trackingEyemart Express operates physical stores and a website where customers can browse products, purchase prescription eyewear and schedule eye exams. According to the complaint, the retailer used Meta Pixel, a tracking tool that collects information about users’ activity on third-party websites and helps Meta build profiles for targeted advertising. The plaintiffs allege that the tool transmitted their website activity to Meta without their knowledge or consent. The five plaintiffs divide themselves into two groups. The Search Plaintiffs say they browsed the website for prescription glasses, triggering the Pixel to track their activity. One of them also alleges that, when she scheduled an eye exam, the tool sent Meta the name and location of the Eyemart store she visited. The Prescription Plaintiffs say they purchased prescription eyewear from Eyemart, entered their prescription information on the website and had that information shared with Meta.All five plaintiffs had Facebook accounts containing personal information, including their names and photographs. They allege that Meta could combine this information with activity tracked on Eyemart’s website to identify them and deliver targeted advertisements. They also allege that Eyemart uploaded customer lists containing email addresses and purchase information, including details of prescription eyewear customers had purchased or viewed, so Meta could match those records to Facebook profiles. The customers sued under the federal Wiretap Act, the Missouri Wiretap Act and the Illinois Eavesdropping Act. They also brought claims involving intrusion upon seclusion and breach of contract. These remain allegations, not established findings of liability. In reviewing the dismissal, the Fifth Circuit accepted the complaint’s factual allegations as true, as required at this stage of litigation.Fifth Circuit ruling on Meta Pixel health data: why the court reversed the dismissalThe panel was Judges Haynes, Higginson and Ho, and Judge Stephen A. Higginson wrote the opinion. The court first addressed standing, the legal requirement that plaintiffs demonstrate a sufficient personal stake in a dispute to bring it before a federal court. Eyemart renewed its argument that the customers lacked standing, but the Fifth Circuit agreed with the district court that the alleged unauthorised disclosure of individually identifiable health information constituted a concrete and particularised injury. It considered the alleged privacy harm comparable to harms recognised in traditional privacy claims. The court therefore held that the plaintiffs had standing to sue.The court then examined the two grounds on which the district court had dismissed the case. The first was that the Search Plaintiffs had not adequately alleged that they shared individually identifiable health information with Eyemart. The second was that the plaintiffs had not adequately alleged that their health information was transmitted to Meta. The Fifth Circuit disagreed on both points. It followed the parties’ approach of using HIPAA’s definition of individually identifiable health information as a framework for assessing the allegations. The court explained that such information need not consist solely of a specific diagnosis or prescription. Information relating to a person’s health or the provision of healthcare services may also fall within the definition when it identifies the individual.The Search Plaintiffs alleged that their searches for prescription eyewear and their interactions with eye-exam scheduling services generated information that the Pixel transmitted to Meta. One plaintiff alleged that the tool shared the name and location of the store she visited when scheduling an appointment. The court concluded that these activities could relate to the plaintiffs’ health and the provision of healthcare services. For the Prescription Plaintiffs, the district court had accepted that they shared health information with Eyemart by entering prescription details but found the allegations of disclosure to Meta insufficient. The appeals court said the lower court had focused too narrowly on sample illustrations in the complaint while overlooking other allegations about tracked product views, purchases, appointment details and customer-list uploads. Taken together, those allegations were sufficient to plead that the Pixel transmitted health-related information to Meta.The court stressed that, without discovery, plaintiffs cannot be expected to know much more at this early stage. It explained that a motion to dismiss tests the sufficiency of the pleadings, not the merits of the case. It did not rule that every element of each claim had been established. Instead, it reversed the dismissal on the two grounds it had considered and remanded the case, sending it back to the district court to reconsider the substantive claims. Discovery will be necessary if the district court finds that the plaintiffs have adequately pleaded the elements of their claims.What the Eyemart ruling means for online retailers and health data privacyThe decision is limited to the issues addressed at the pleading stage. Eyemart Express can continue to contest the claims in the district court, where the evidence and remaining legal questions can be examined. Meta is not a party to this appeal, which concerns the retailer’s alleged conduct. The case also sits within wider scrutiny of tracking technologies used on websites dealing with health information. The US Department of Health and Human Services has published guidance titled Use of Online Tracking Technologies by HIPAA Covered Entities and Business Associates, outlining obligations for organisations regulated by HIPAA when using online tracking tools.That guidance has faced a legal challenge. On June 20, 2024, a federal district court in American Hospital Association v. Becerra vacated part of the guidance concerning circumstances in which an online technology connects an individual’s IP address with a visit to an unauthenticated public webpage addressing a specific health condition or healthcare provider. The Fifth Circuit noted that decision but distinguished the allegations in Rand, which involved claims that more extensive website activity was linked to identifiable Facebook users. The ruling may be relevant to retailers that sell healthcare-related products or facilitate appointments through websites using advertising trackers. Eyemart provides vision-care products and services, and the court said that activity on its website therefore pertains to customers’ vision.The decision is a pleading-stage ruling from the Fifth Circuit, whose jurisdiction covers Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi. It does not establish a nationwide rule that every visit to an eyewear website constitutes the disclosure of protected health information, nor does it determine whether Eyemart is ultimately liable. The next stage of the case will depend on the district court’s assessment of the plaintiffs’ substantive claims and, if those claims are adequately pleaded, the evidence obtained through discovery.You use AI every day. articles.title: Hasina video, RAW allegations: What ex-Bangladesh officer revealed in podcast before mysterious death
articles.summary: A former Bangladesh air force officer was found dead near Turag River in Dhaka on Wednesday, weeks after his podcast questioning allegations linking him
articles.body: A former Bangladesh air force officer was found dead near Turag River in Dhaka on Wednesday, weeks after his podcast questioning allegations linking him to a video purportedly showing former prime minister Sheikh Hasina fleeing the country in August 2024.The 28-year-old former flight lieutenant Tahsif Souri had gone missing a day before his body was recovered. Police said an inquest report found no external injury marks on his body, though blood was seen coming out of his nose.His body was sent to Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College for an autopsy.Souri had been "compulsorily retired" from service about a year after the fall of the Hasina government.His death has brought renewed attention to a podcast interview in which he spoke about allegations that he had recorded and circulated footage of Hasina leaving Bangladesh on August 5, 2024.The interview resurfaced following the recovery of his body.What ex-Bangladesh officer said about allegationsDuring the interview as cited by the Dhaka Tribune, the host referred to a media report alleging that footage of Hasina leaving the country had been recorded at Kurmitola Airport and circulated by Souri. The report had also reportedly linked him to an investigation into the alleged involvement of the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), within the Bangladesh air force.Responding to the allegations, Souri said the report had claimed that flight lieutenant Rifat Ashrafi recorded the video and that he had circulated it. He questioned the evidence behind the claim that he had shared the footage.“Even if I recorded the video or circulated it, what proof do they have? I want to ask that,” he said.Asked whether the allegations had led to his dismissal from the air force, Souri said this was possible but declined to disclose details of the events at the time.“I cannot disclose everything, and there are things I am unable to discuss. I think they did this because of these allegations,” he said.Souri also said he faced social embarrassment and harassment after the report was published, claiming its headline and presentation had created a misleading impression of him among readers.He rejected allegations of RAW's involvement within the air force, saying: “If I were linked to RAW, why would I be in Bangladesh? If I were linked to RAW, why would I speak publicly?”He described the allegation as “a very ridiculous claim”.Souri further claimed that the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) directorate had said he had no such involvement. However, no detailed documents supporting the claim were presented during the interview.Asked whether he had appealed against his discharge from the air force, Souri said he had not and was uncertain whether he would do so in the future.He also expressed frustration over the withholding of his passport, describing it as a violation of his democratic rights.“They had withheld my passport, which is my democratic right. I am deeply upset about this. I suffered for two years,” he said, adding that he had since recovered the passport.Souri's interview prompted the military's public relations directorate, ISPR, to reiterate its August 4, 2025, statement. It had denied reports that action against Souri and flight lieutenant Rifat Ashrafi was linked to allegations that the officers had recorded and shared the video showing Hasina fleeing the country.During the podcast, Souri dismissed as propaganda a 2024 media report claiming he was an agent of RAW. However, he neither confirmed nor denied his alleged links to the video.Souri's father, KM Enayetul Karim Helal, told reporters that an acquaintance, Dwip, had taken his son out on Tuesday evening."Tahsif sent his mother a message round 1:30am Wednesday, saying he would return home. But he never did" said Helal.Bangladesh home minister Salahuddin Ahmed told reporters that he would comment after the initial probe and autopsy findings. He did not respond when asked whether Souri had shot the video.Meanwhile, Ashraful Alam Khokan, a former aide of Hasina, questioned whether Souri had been deliberately targeted through media reports."Was Tahsif deliberately portrayed in the media as an agent of RAW with the intention of getting him killed? "At the time, however, his activities were reportedly aligned with those who seized power in July," he said, referring to the Muhammad Yunus-led government.You use AI every day. articles.title: Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
articles.summary: The government is under pressure to set out a path to greater defence spending, as ministers unveil plans to boost UK firms.
articles.body:
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has denied "kicking the can down the road" over how much the UK spends on defence.

The government has faced criticism for not setting out a pathway at Wednesday's Budget to hit its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

Streeting is at odds with MPs on the Commons defence committee over the issue.

It comes as Chancellor John Healey and Streeting announce that foreign firms which are awarded defence contracts of more than £50m will need to invest an equal value back into the UK.

Under the new investment rules, described as an "offset strategy", these companies will need to spend an equivalent amount on British factories, jobs and training.

The Ministry of Defence will apply the rules on a "case-by-case" basis from April 2027, the government said. Healey and Streeting will unveil the policy on a visit to UK defence contractor BAE's shipbuilding site in Glasgow later.

Countries including Poland, Norway and the Netherlands have mandated similar rules to "boost the economic benefit from defence procurement", the government said.

While ministers hope the rules increase investment in Britain's defence industry, they appear designed to do so in a politically palatable way rather than committing to spending cuts.

Tan Dhesi, Labour chair of the cross-party Commons defence committee, said on Wednesday that decisions had been "kicked into the long grass" to next year's government spending review, rather than announced in the Budget .

He warned that without building capabilities now, "we risk leaving ourselves seriously vulnerable in the event of a major conflict".

Streeting hit back at these comments as "unfair" and "unfounded".

Speaking on Thursday, Dhesi said the committee stands by its criticism.

"We had hoped to see that the chancellor would set out a precise pathway to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030," Dhesi told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"But instead some of those key decisions on defence have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review."

He praised the government for plugging a £4.7bn hole in the Defence Investment Plan in the Budget, through asking government departments to cut their capital budgets by 1% .

Responding on Thursday, Streeting told Today: "I like Tan very much, he's a friend and I respect him, but I strongly disagree with him.

"And I don't think the charge he makes of delaying or kicking the can down the road stacks up against the extra money that is already going into defence and the capability we're funding right now."

Streeting told BBC Breakfast the new rules, aiming to create "bang for the British buck", would help achieve this target given increasing defence spending "does come at a cost to the country and other things we'd like to spend money on".

He said waiting for the spending review, which does not have a fixed date and could come in the second half of 2027, was "the right thing to do" so ministers can look at "spending in the round".

He added that the UK was ready to deal with hostile threats, but "we're not where we'd want to be".

"There's no sugarcoating the fact that our Armed Forces were under-invested in for more than a decade," he told Breakfast.

Defence analysts have questioned the government's ability to deliver on its 2030 target and the Nato-wide target of 3.5% by 2035. UK defence spending is at an estimated 2.6% of GDP this year.

Some estimates have suggested the government will need to spend an additional £10bn annually to reach its targets.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said on Wednesday that Healey "failed his own test" by not setting out a "plan for 3%".

Healey resigned as then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June over not spending enough on defence.

In the Budget, Healey said the UK was negotiating with Finland, Poland and the Netherlands to set up an international bank - the Multilateral Defence Mechanism - to boost defence investment and joint procurement.

But Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge said this amounted to "turning to borrowing at a time when the national debt is over £3 trillion".

"The answer is not more borrowing – it's to cut welfare to fund defence," he said.

articles.title: 'A win is a win': Israel opposition leader Lapid reacts to Netanyahu's poll setback
articles.summary: Israel’s outgoing opposition leader Yair Lapid, who is also the second most prominent leader in the B’Yachad alliance, has claimed that the anti-Netanyahu
articles.body: Israel’s outgoing opposition leader Yair Lapid, who is also the second most prominent leader in the B’Yachad alliance, has claimed that the anti-Netanyahu bloc “won” the election, even though it fell short of an outright victory. He called on the public to be patient while the bloc looks for ways to form a government.“It's not a knockout victory. It's a points victory. That counts too. A win is a win,” Lapid said.The anti-Netanyahu bloc took a combined 67 seats in the 120-member Knesset, but reaching a majority of 61 is difficult.Three of the four Jewish-led parties in the bloc (Yashar, B’Yachad and Yisrael Beytenu) have rejected the idea of sitting in a coalition with the predominantly Arab Joint List and Ra’am. The Times of Israel reported.Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats, and his Likud party became the largest single party with 27. Still, Netanyahu also lacks a clear route to the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.In a post on X, Lapid said that Netanyahu’s opponents had hoped for “a clear, immediate victory”, but maintained that the outcome should nonetheless be seen as a win for the opposition.“Netanyahu got 53 seats. A crash. Even from that small number, 13 seats belong to parties that declare they aren't Zionist,” he wrote, referring to the ultra-Orthodox parties United Torah Judaism and Shas, which won seven and six seats, respectively.“That leaves him 40 [seats],” Lapid said, contending that Netanyahu had no path to forming a government. “So we won,” he declared, calling the result “a win on points” instead of a knockout victory.Lapid said the opposition bloc, headed by Yashar chair Gadi Eisenkot, would use every means available to form a government, though he admitted the process would be hard and success was not assured.He requested “patience” from the public, explaining that forming a government is the opposite of an election campaign and happens behind closed doors, out of view of the cameras.“I know the human race hates uncertainty, but think how much you'd hate finding out in another month that for the sake of a headline or some leak, we didn't work smart, quiet, and precise,” he wrote.Lapid added that talks were taking place even though nothing had been announced publicly. “If you want to know if something's happening behind the silence you're hearing now, the answer is yes,” he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Manchester United Munich air disaster memorial vandalised
articles.summary: Four medals and a crystal trophy were taken from the display, according to German media.
articles.body:
A glass sculpture and medals have been stolen from a memorial to the 23 people killed in the Munich air disaster, including eight Manchester United players.

The items were taken from a display case at Manchesterplatz in Munich, where the plane crashed on take-off on 6 February 1958 after refuelling on its return from a European Cup match in Belgrade.

Munich Police told German media the glass was smashed with a stone and said the incident was believed to have happened between 08:00 and 13:00 local time on Monday, 26 October.

The Manchester Munich Memorial Foundation (MMMF) said it was "deeply saddened", while its chair, Ifty Ahmed, said the theft had caused emotional harm to families.

"They don't understand the damage that they've caused," Ahmed told BBC News.

He said the memorial had provided solace for families who lost loved ones in the crash.

"And whatever they've taken from inside the showcase, they haven't taken our memories," he said.

Mark Salzmann, chairman of Red Docs Munich, a Bayern Munich supporters' group which helps care for the memorial, said his mother discovered the damage while driving past.

Salzmann said a glass sculpture originally presented to Munich's former mayor, Dieter Reiter, was among the stolen items.

His group collects tributes left by visitors from around the world and places some of them in the display case.

He said the objects were unique and could not easily be replaced, but the group was discussing possible replacements with the foundation.

Ahmed said it was still unclear exactly how many medals were missing.

He said Manchester United had offered to pay for repairs, but the foundation had already agreed to cover the costs itself.

The broken glass was replaced on the same day, according to the foundation.

Ahmed said supporters of Liverpool, Manchester City and Leeds had also sent messages of support.

A memorial stone was installed in 2004, while the display case was added in 2020 and officially inaugurated in 2023.

About 1,500 people from around the world attended the annual remembrance service at Manchesterplatz in February, according to the foundation.

Salzmann said the messages of support he had received showed how important the memorial was, adding that the connection between Manchester and Munich "will never go away".

The BBC has contacted Munich Police and Manchester United for comment.

articles.title: An Idaho couple who have farmed beside a barbed-wire fence since 1979 fought the state over 5.95 acres, and an October 27 Supreme Court ruling reversed the state's title victory and reopened their ownership claim
articles.summary: An Idaho couple who have farmed in Benewah County since 1979 have won another chance to claim 5.95 acres of disputed land after the state Supreme Court
articles.body: An Idaho couple who have farmed in Benewah County since 1979 have won another chance to claim 5.95 acres of disputed land after the state Supreme Court overturned an earlier ruling in Idaho's favour on Tuesday. Greg and Leah Sempel believed the land was theirs because an old barbed-wire fence had marked their property's boundary for decades. However, the state claims the land belongs to it and sued the couple in 2022 over its alleged unauthorised use.According to the judgment, the couple run Pokey Creek Farm, where they have grown crops, kept animals and built structures over the years. They say the land inside the fence was theirs because that was what they had been told when the property was purchased. They said the fence had been there long before they arrived, and they continued to treat it as the boundary.The state, however, has documents showing that the disputed 5.95 acres are part of a much larger property it acquired in 1996. But the Sempels argue that they had already been using the area for many years before the state became its owner. With the Supreme Court's latest ruling, the competing claim will be examined again.The disputed barbed-wire fenceThe story began in 1979, when Greg's parents purchased the property for him and Leah to use. Before the purchase, Greg said he walked around the land with Tom Rathbone, a representative of the company selling it. During that visit, Rathbone pointed towards a barbed-wire fence and told him it marked the northern boundary.Greg later spoke to Chester Henning, who had owned the property previously. According to Greg, Henning told him that the fence had been built in the 1960s after an agreement with the company that owned the neighbouring land.The couple say they had followed that boundary ever since. In their early years, they planted crops and kept horses in the area. During the 1980s, they harvested timber, laid a gravel access road and built several structures. In the following decade, they added a greenhouse and raised livestock.They also claimed that government workers carrying out logging operations had treated the fence as the dividing line between the properties.How state came to claim the landWhile the Sempels continued farming, the neighbouring property changed hands. It belonged to Milwaukee Land Company until 1981, when Potlatch Corporation acquired it. In December 1996, Potlatch transferred more than 4,100 acres to the State of Idaho through a land exchange. The disputed 5.95 acres were included in that transfer.Years later, a survey carried out in 2016 raised questions about the couple's use of the land. The state claimed that they were occupying part of its property without permission.In August 2022, Idaho took the couple to court. Apart from asking the court to recognise its ownership, it sought compensation over the alleged unauthorised use of the land, timber removal and property damage.Couple refuse to give up landThe Sempels said they had been using the disputed area openly since 1979 and had treated it as part of their farm. They relied on a legal principle known as adverse possession, which can allow someone to claim ownership of land they have occupied for a required period, provided certain conditions are satisfied. The couple argued that they had met those conditions by 1984, long before the state acquired the property.They also maintained that the fence was not simply something built to keep animals inside. According to their account, it had been accepted as the boundary by previous landowners. The lower court, however, ruled in the state's favour on the ownership dispute.On the issue of property taxes, Greg said he and Leah had always paid taxes on their property, but the lower court found that they had not provided enough evidence to establish it. The couple challenged that decision in the Supreme Court.What changed in Supreme CourtThe Supreme Court found that the lower court had dismissed important parts of the couple's case without properly considering the evidence.For example, Greg had given a sworn statement saying they had paid their property taxes. Although older receipts were unavailable, the judges said that statement could not simply be treated as though no evidence had been presented.The court also considered whether taxes paid on the couple's recorded property could count towards the disputed area under an exception recognised by Idaho law.Photographs showed that some sections of the wire fence had become embedded in trees as they grew. The state argued that the fence was irregularly shaped and had fallen into disrepair. However, the judges said its present condition did not establish what it looked like when the couple first occupied the property or whether earlier landowners had accepted it as the boundary.For now, neither side has secured a final victory in the ownership dispute. The Supreme Court has sent the case back for further proceedings, where the couple's claims will have to be considered again.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2023, a California couple began a divorce with competing requests for protection orders; three years later, a court overturned the husband's $39,000 legal-fee award because he filed too late
articles.summary: A California man who was awarded $39,000 in legal fees from his wife during their divorce proceedings will no longer receive the money after an appeals
articles.body: A California man who was awarded $39,000 in legal fees from his wife during their divorce proceedings will no longer receive the money after an appeals court found on Wednesday that he had waited too long to make the claim.The couple's dispute began in 2023, when the husband filed for divorce and sought a restraining order against his wife. She later asked the court for a similar order against him. Although the two settled their dispute over the restraining orders in January 2024, the husband returned to court more than a year later seeking payment for his lawyers. The California Court of Appeal ruled that his request had come too late and overturned the award.According to the judgment, the case involved a man identified in court documents as A O and his wife, Alina Vologodskaya. When A O started the divorce proceedings, he also wanted his wife to pay some or all of his legal expenses. Vologodskaya responded by seeking protection from him and asking for financial support.By January 2024, both sides were preparing to argue their cases in court. A O wanted a restraining order lasting five years, while his wife had asked for one lasting three years. However, instead of going ahead with the planned hearing, they reached an agreement.They settled their competing requests for protection and made arrangements for financial support. But one important matter was missing: neither side said what should happen to the money spent on lawyers. That omission later became central to the dispute over the $39,000 award.What happened when the couple settled their dispute?Under the settlement, Vologodskaya agreed to a one-year restraining order protecting her husband. She also acknowledged committing at least one act of domestic abuse that justified the order and withdrew her own request for protection.The couple also agreed on how some of their expenses would be handled while the divorce continued. A O would pay temporary spousal support, while Vologodskaya would pay her own rent and monthly car instalments.They further agreed that each would receive $50,000 in advance from their shared marital property. Any questions about future bonuses or additional income affecting support payments could be decided by the court later.The settlement was recorded in court, and the written orders were filed. However, the documents did not specifically leave the question of legal fees open for another hearing. In fact, one document indicated that no decision on legal fees was applicable, while the relevant space in another was left empty. For more than a year, there was no further decision on the husband's request for legal expenses.Husband returns to court seeking over $75,000In April 2025, A.O. asked the court to make Vologodskaya pay $75,476 towards his legal expenses.His argument was that he had succeeded in obtaining protection from his wife and had also defended himself against her attempt to secure a restraining order. He believed these outcomes entitled him to recover the money spent on lawyers.Vologodskaya challenged the demand, but her objection was not about how much he had spent. She argued that he had missed the deadline for asking the court to order payment.Despite her objection, the lower court ruled in the husband's favour. After hearing arguments in October and December 2025, it awarded him $39,000 in February 2026.The wife then appealed, bringing the question of whether the husband had filed his claim on time before a higher court.Why did the appeals court reject the husband's claim?The California Court of Appeal examined the rules governing when a person can ask for legal fees after a court decision. Under the rule applicable to this case, such a request had to be made within the period allowed for appealing the restraining order decision. That period could extend to a maximum of 180 days.For A O, the problem was the gap between the original court order and his later application. The restraining order had been issued in February 2024, but he did not seek the $75,476 until April 2025, roughly 14 months later.The husband pointed out that he had requested legal fees at the beginning of the case and that the earlier court documents contained general wording allowing other matters to be considered later.But the appeals court found a difference between mentioning legal fees in an earlier application and specifically keeping that issue open after a settlement.The judges observed that the couple had clearly agreed to leave certain financial questions for future consideration. They had not done the same for legal fees, even though both had lawyers when the agreement was reached.A O also maintained that the deadline should not apply while the divorce proceedings remained unfinished. The appeals court rejected this argument because the restraining order dispute had already been resolved, regardless of whether the marriage had been legally dissolved.He also wanted the lower court to consider extending the deadline. However, the judges found that he had not raised that request when the lower court was hearing the matter.The appeals court thus concluded that the husband had submitted his legal-fee request after the permitted period and that the lower court should not have awarded him the money.It therefore cancelled the February 23 order directing Vologodskaya to pay $39,000. The judges also decided that each side would pay its own expenses arising from the appeal.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: An anonymous Connecticut family donated $50 million to a global health charity; the record gift will expand access to lifesaving medicines, support healthcare centres and secure the organisation's financial future
articles.summary: An anonymous family from Connecticut has donated $50 million to Americares, a global health and disaster-relief organisation, in the largest gift in its
articles.body: An anonymous family from Connecticut has donated $50 million to Americares, a global health and disaster-relief organisation, in the largest gift in its history. Announced on September 9, 2026, the donation will help expand access to essential medicines, strengthen partnerships with healthcare providers and improve the long-term resilience of health systems. The family has supported the organisation for 30 years, and the contribution comes as cuts to international aid funding put pressure on healthcare programmes worldwide. The donation will be distributed over five years, with half earmarked for expanding healthcare access and the other half allocated to Americares' endowment to help sustain its work in the years ahead.How Americares plans to use the $50 million donationThe donation will support Americares' five-year strategy to improve access to healthcare, particularly in communities affected by poverty, disasters and fragile medical systems.According to the organisation's announcement, $25 million will support healthcare expansion, including its Access to Medicine programme. The remaining $25 million will strengthen its endowment, providing a stronger financial foundation for its long-term work.The healthcare component will help Americares expand medicine distribution, strengthen local healthcare partnerships and improve the reliability of medical supply chains. The organisation aims to ensure that patients and healthcare facilities can obtain essential treatments when they need them.The gift will also support Americares' goal of helping 100 million people access quality healthcare by 2030.Which countries and communities will benefit?Americares plans to expand its medicine-access work in high-need countries across sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and North Africa, Asia, and Latin America. These regions include communities where fragile healthcare systems and persistent shortages of medicines can prevent patients from receiving appropriate treatment.The organisation also intends to increase support for safety-net health centres in the United States. These facilities provide healthcare to people who are uninsured or underinsured, and Americares plans to focus on states where policy changes are expected to increase the number of residents without health insurance.The donation is intended to strengthen existing healthcare networks rather than establish an entirely new system. By working with local providers, Americares aims to improve access to medicines and make healthcare delivery more reliable.Americares supports more than 4,000 health centres worldwideFounded in 1979, Americares is a US-based nonprofit that provides medicines, medical supplies, emergency assistance and health services to communities around the world.The organisation supports more than 4,000 health centres globally, working with local partners to improve access to treatment and strengthen healthcare systems. Its activities include distributing donated medicines, responding to natural disasters and humanitarian emergencies, and supporting long-term health programmes.In the year before the donation announcement, Americares delivered approximately $1.8 billion in aid. This included enough medicine to fill nine million prescriptions and three million medical supplies for patients in need, according to its September announcement.The organisation also responds to emergencies and helps communities restore essential health services after disasters. Its work spans both immediate humanitarian relief and longer-term efforts to improve the capacity of local healthcare providers.Why the donation comes amid global aid cutsThe $50 million gift comes at a time when reductions in international aid funding have disrupted healthcare programmes in several countries.According to the Associated Press, Americares has lost support for projects including a maternal-care programme in Tanzania. Medical clinics in Colombia serving Venezuelan migrants also closed after private funders had supported them for several months.The funding pressures have affected a wider range of humanitarian services, including maternal and child healthcare, HIV treatment and prevention, and medical assistance for vulnerable populations.Americares had previously received some funding from the US government, which accounted for approximately 10% of its funding before recent aid cuts, the Associated Press reported. The organisation has since continued its work through a mix of individual donors, corporations and private foundations.The new donation will provide additional resources for its healthcare expansion plans while strengthening its ability to sustain programmes over time.Half the donation will strengthen Americares' endowmentOne of the defining features of the gift is the decision to allocate $25 million to Americares' endowment rather than direct healthcare expansion.An endowment is a pool of financial assets intended to support an organisation over the long term. It can help generate income for future activities and reduce dependence on short-term grants or individual funding commitments.For a humanitarian organisation, financial stability can be particularly important because healthcare programmes require consistent supplies, staffing and support. Interruptions in funding can affect a clinic's ability to maintain services or provide patients with essential medicines.By increasing its endowment, Americares intends to strengthen its financial resilience and protect its capacity to deliver healthcare in the future. The remaining $25 million will support the expansion of its healthcare work, creating a balance between immediate programme needs and long-term sustainability.Anonymous family has supported Americares for 30 yearsAmericares said the donation came from a philanthropic Connecticut family that has supported the organisation for approximately three decades. The family has chosen not to disclose its identity publicly.Christine Squires, president and CEO of Americares, said the family understood the challenges facing global health and wanted to do more in response to the growing needs.The organisation described the contribution as a significant investment in its five-year strategic plan, which includes expanding its network of local healthcare partners, improving access to medicines and strengthening emergency-response capabilities.Americares also hopes the record-breaking gift will encourage other philanthropists to support humanitarian healthcare initiatives as organisations face mounting pressure to maintain essential services.You use AI every day. articles.title: Neanderthals made three-ply cord by twisting tree bark fibres, a tiny fragment found on a stone tool in France reveals
articles.summary: A fragment of cord found on a stone tool in a rock shelter has provided evidence that Neanderthals made fibre-based materials during the Middle
articles.body: A fragment of cord found on a stone tool in a rock shelter has provided evidence that Neanderthals made fibre-based materials during the Middle Palaeolithic. Researchers identified the remains as a three-ply cord made from inner bark fibres. It was attached to a stone flake recovered at Abri du Maras in south-eastern France.According to research published in Scientific Reports titled ‘Direct evidence of Neanderthal fibre technology and its cognitive and behavioral implications’, the cord was formed from bundles of twisted plant fibres. The researchers said twisted fibres could have been used to make clothing, rope, bags, nets, mats and boats.Ancient cord fragment found beneath the surface at a French rock shelterThe cord fragment was discovered on the underside of a Levallois flake known as G8 128. The stone tool came from archaeological level 4.2 at Abri du Maras, a rock shelter in south-eastern France. It was found in place, about three metres below the modern surface. The researchers said the cord entered the deposit at the same time as, or before, the flake.The surrounding sediment and breccia covered the artefact. The excavation team kept it unwashed in a plastic bag until it could be examined under a microscope. This handling helped rule out modern contamination. The cord measured about 6.2 millimetres long and 0.5 millimetres wide. Unit 4 contained more than 4,000 artefacts longer than 15 mm across its two archaeological levels.How did researchers identify the source of the ancient fibresResearchers examined the fragment using reflected-light microscopy, scanning electron microscopy and a digital microscope. The images showed three bundles of fibres twisted in an S direction. These bundles were then combined with a Z twist to form a three-ply cord. The structure closely resembled replica cords made using modern materials.The team also examined the fibres' microscopic features to identify their source. Bordered pits with torus-margo membranes appeared in parallel lines, a pattern associated with conifer wood. The researchers noted that the fibres likely came from the inner bark of a conifer. Pine was present at Abri du Maras, according to pollen and charcoal evidence from the site. None of the 18 modern fibre samples collected matched the ancient material.What the cord reveals about Neanderthal behaviourThe authors said making the cord would have involved more than twisting plant material. It required combining several fibres and strands in a set arrangement. They argued that understanding and using twisted fibres involved complex, multi-component technology. The process also implied an understanding of pairs, sets and numbers.The researchers suggested that such knowledge may have been needed to produce cordage and make objects from it. The study adds to evidence about Neanderthal behaviour alongside discoveries of birch bark tar, art and shell beads.Significance of the ancient cord fragmentThe researchers said twisted fibres form the basis of many objects, including clothing, rope, bags, nets, mats and boats. These materials can be made from plant fibres, but they rarely survive in archaeological deposits. As a result, the material record from Palaeolithic sites often contains stone tools and animal remains while perishable objects are missing. Earlier work at Abri du Maras had identified individual twisted fibres on stone tools.However, those remains were too fragmentary to confirm that they came from cordage. The newly identified fragment was different because it preserved a clear structure of multiple plies. The authors described it as direct evidence of fibre technology among Neanderthals.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
articles.summary: Novaya Gazeta has been one of the most high-profile independent news outlets in Russia over the last three decades.
articles.body:
For the last three decades, Novaya Gazeta has been one of the most high-profile independent news outlets in Russia.

Now it's shutting down - and it has accused the Russian authorities of the "murder" of a newspaper.

"They've killed us," reads a statement on the Novaya Gazeta website.

"The newspaper is no more. The Russian authorities and Russian special services have forced the paper to stop its work."

Novaya Gazeta has received an eviction order. Crucially, at the same time, the system that had allowed the paper to receive donations from readers was disabled.

That leaves no way to fund the publication.

Novaya Gazeta had developed a reputation for fearless investigative reporting on subjects such as corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power by officials and bureaucrats.

The paper said that over time six journalists connected with the paper were killed for "fulfilling their professional and civic duty." Those reporters include Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot dead in the stairwell of her apartment block 20 years ago this month. Among the subjects she had reported on were the wars in Chechnya.

In the statement announcing its closure, Novaya Gazeta launched a stinging attack on the Russian authorities, claiming the newspaper was the victim of a "coordinated act" and blaming "the repressive state apparatus".

"Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in the country and their protection has been equated to a crime," the statement said.

"The courts have been destroyed along with the law. Having convictions is now state treason."

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the pressure on independent journalism and independent Russian journalists has been growing. Soon after the start of what the Kremlin calls the so-called "special military operation", new laws were adopted in Russia. Their aim: to punish dissent and silence criticism of the war and of those in power.

Novaya Gazeta itself and its staff had been facing a multitude of problems.

The authorities had already revoked the newspaper's licence and blocked access to its website. Several of its journalists and contributors had been designated "foreign agents", a label often used by the Russian authorities to punish critics.

Earlier this year there was a police search of the editorial office. A veteran investigative journalist, Oleg Roldugin, was arrested and charged with "unlawful access to computerised information". In connection with the case, the newspaper's editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, was recently taken in for police questioning and his home was searched.

Despite increasing pressure, Novaya Gazeta had managed to continue operating, albeit in a reduced form. Loyal readers used virtual private networks to circumvent official blocking of the website and access content. But the loss of its licence and other restrictions dealt a major blow.

One of the founders of Novaya Gazeta in the 1990s - and for many years its chief editor - was journalist Dmitry Muratov . In 2021, Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression, which is a precondition for democracy and lasting peace".

The award didn't stop the authorities from declaring him a "foreign agent" in 2023.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A Rafale Marine fighter jet successfully landed on Indian Navy's indigenous aircraft carrier INS Vikrant on its maiden attempt during ongoing
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Rafale Marine fighter jet successfully landed on Indian Navy's indigenous aircraft carrier INS Vikrant on its maiden attempt during ongoing trials in Goa, the force said.The Navy shared a video of the landing on its official X handle on Friday, a day after the successful landing.Also Read: Rafale Marine trials underway in Goa for INS Vikrant operations"A Rafale Marine aircraft successfully landed onboard Indian Navy's indigenous Aircraft Carrier #INSVikrant on its maiden attempt on 29 Oct 26. The ongoing trials mark the first steps towards operationalisation of the aircraft in the Indian Navy," the Navy said in its post, accompanying the video.The ongoing trials are aimed at validating modifications required to operate the French-origin aircraft from the carrier. The Navy has signed a contract for 26 Rafale Marine jets, with deliveries expected by the end of 2028 or early 2029.Why are the trials significantThe trials are significant as the Rafale Marine, also known as Rafale M, was originally designed to operate from CATOBAR (Catapult Assisted Take-Off But Arrested Recovery) aircraft carriers. INS Vikrant, however, uses the STOBAR (Short Take-Off But Arrested Recovery) system, under which fighter jets take off using a ski-jump ramp and land by engaging arrestor wires on the flight deck.Integrating the Rafale M with INS Vikrant, therefore, requires extensive testing to validate the aircraft's compatibility with the carrier's ski-jump launch configuration, arrestor-wire recovery system and other onboard infrastructure.About Rafale MarineThe Rafale M is a carrier-based, twin-engine multirole fighter developed by French aerospace manufacturer Dassault Aviation for the French Navy. It can perform air defence, reconnaissance, deep-strike and anti-ship missions.Powered by two Safran M88 engines, the aircraft can reach speeds of up to Mach 1.8 (around 2,200 kmph). It features an arrestor hook for aircraft carrier landings and advanced radar and electronic warfare systems.Its weapons package includes Meteor and MICA air-to-air missiles, SCALP cruise missiles and AM39 Exocet anti-ship missiles.

articles.title: Paul Heaton to headline at Ludlow Castle in July
articles.summary: The Beautiful South and The Housemartins singer is the latest act to be announced for next summer.
articles.body:
Former Housemartins frontman Paul Heaton is set to perform in beautiful south Shropshire next year.

Heaton will be joined by Scottish singer-songwriter Rianne Downey on 17 July, when he plays as part of the annual summer concert series in Ludlow.

The Live at Ludlow Castle shows will also feature McFly, Becky Hill and UB40 ft Ali Campbell, with more acts due to be announced.

The concerts began in 2023, with 50,000 people visiting this year over two weekends, to see the likes of Snow Patrol, Paul Weller, The Human League, Tom Grennan, The Streets, Rick Astley, Richard Ashcroft and Scissor Sisters.

Heaton founded The Housemartins in 1983 and found success with Happy Hour, Caravan of Love and Build.

Later, he created The Beautiful South, who released 10 albums and had chart success with songs including A Little Time, Don't Marry Her and others.

The band sold 15 million albums and their 1994 singles compilation, Carry On Up The Charts, has been one of the best-selling albums in British history.

Since The Beautiful South broke up Heaton has continued as a solo artist and during the coronavirus pandemic he discovered Downey after she posted a video of herself singing The Beautiful South's single, Rotterdam (Or Anywhere).

The pair now tour together and have appeared at festivals including Radio 2 in the Park and Glastonbury.

Support acts for Heaton are yet to be announced.

The Live at Ludlow organisers, Futuresound, said the concerts sell out every year and had become "a vital and highly anticipated event in the town's cultural calendar".

Futuresound said they brought more than £1m into the town in 2025 and an agreement was signed this summer to continue them until at least 2033.

Tickets for the Paul Heaton concert are due to go on sale to people in the Ludlow area on 4 November with general sale starting on 6 November.

articles.title: A Georgia couple won a $37 million jury verdict after their three-year-old son died during hospital treatment, but a judge cut it to $2 million; an October 28 appeals ruling now raises the judgment to $3 million
articles.summary: A couple in Georgia, US, has secured a higher compensation judgment after an appeals court revisited a case involving the death of their three-year-old
articles.body: A couple in Georgia, US, has secured a higher compensation judgment after an appeals court revisited a case involving the death of their three-year-old son during hospital treatment. In a ruling dated October 28, 2026, the Georgia Court of Appeals directed the trial court to enter a $3 million damages judgment against the Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia, reversing a previous reduction of the family's $37 million jury verdict to $2 million. The ruling, published by Justia in Warren et al. v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia, addresses how state law limits compensation in cases involving public institutions. It does not restore the original jury award or reinstate every claim brought by the parents.The case centres on the treatment of the couple's son, identified in the judgment as B.W., at Augusta University Medical Center in 2016. His parents, Bryce Warren and April Bradshaw, took him to the hospital on June 23 that year after noticing an abdominal mass and consulting physicians in their hometown of Moultrie, Georgia. They initially believed he might have a blockage. Instead, doctors diagnosed him with stage-four Burkitt lymphoma, an aggressive form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. According to the court's account, the parents were told that the cancer was “99 percent curable” and that the child needed surgery to insert a port for chemotherapy.The child was moved to the paediatric intensive care unit following surgery. During the first week of chemotherapy, his tumour reportedly decreased in size by 40%, offering some initial encouragement to his family. However, his condition subsequently deteriorated, leading to the medical care that became central to the lawsuit.Skin complications and a delayed consultationAccording to the appellate judgment, doctors began administering allopurinol on July 4, 2016, to manage tumour lysis syndrome, a complication that can occur when cancer cells break down and release substances that affect the body's organs. The following day, the child began experiencing skin sloughing, in which the skin peels away. A wound nurse recommended a dermatology consultation on July 5, but the court record says the physicians did not arrange one until July 12. During that interval, the child received seven additional doses of allopurinol.The dermatologist ultimately diagnosed Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, severe conditions that can cause extensive skin damage and are commonly associated with medication reactions or infections. The allopurinol was discontinued on July 12. The judgment also records that the child developed other serious complications, including sepsis, a urinary infection, skin lesions and fluid accumulation around the lungs.Later on July 12, he struggled to maintain an open airway, and his oxygen levels fell. A medical resident intubated him, but an accidental extubation occurred. A second accidental extubation followed several hours later. The next morning, the child lost his pulse, suffered repeated cardiac arrests and died.His death certificate listed Burkitt lymphoma, hyperkalemia, or elevated potassium levels, and sepsis as causes of death. It did not list Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. His parents sued the Board of Regents, alleging wrongful death and seeking compensation for the child's suffering and their own emotional distress.Jury awards $37 millionThe case went to trial in April 2024, with the Board of Regents the only remaining defendant. After an eight-day trial, the jury returned a verdict in favour of the parents on May 1, awarding $37 million in damages. The award comprised $10 million for the child's pain and suffering, $22 million for his wrongful death and $5 million for his parents' emotional distress.Following the verdict, the Board of Regents sought to reduce the award under the Georgia Tort Claims Act, which limits the amount that can be recovered from state entities. The trial court agreed, reducing the total damages judgment to $2 million: $1 million for the child's estate and $1 million for the wrongful-death claim jointly held by his parents.The trial court also granted the board's motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict on the parents' emotional-distress claims, effectively setting aside that portion of the jury's award. The parents challenged these decisions before the Court of Appeals.Why the judgment increased to $3 millionThe appeals court focused on how Georgia's damages cap applies to the parents' wrongful-death claim. Under the Georgia Tort Claims Act, an individual generally cannot recover more than $1 million for losses arising from a single occurrence involving a state entity, while the state's aggregate liability per occurrence cannot exceed $3 million.The trial court had treated the parents as a single person for the purposes of the wrongful-death claim, limiting their joint recovery to $1 million. The appeals court disagreed, finding that the mother and father are separate legal persons under the statute and that each can recover up to $1 million, subject to the overall cap.Because the child's estate was already entitled to $1 million, the court directed the trial court to enter a total damages judgment of $3 million: $1 million for the estate and $1 million for each parent on the wrongful-death claim.The court did not accept the parents' argument that multiple alleged failures in care should count as separate occurrences, which could have supported a substantially higher recovery. It also upheld the dismissal of their emotional-distress claims and left the trial court's refusal to backdate the judgment unchanged.The appeals court vacated the denial of the parents' request for attorney's fees and expenses and sent that issue back to the trial court for reconsideration.You use AI every day. articles.title: Car driver who dragged head teacher to his death guilty of murder
articles.summary: Simon Richardson is convicted of murdering head teacher Michael Mullins and will be sentenced on Monday.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains distressing content

A man has been found guilty of murdering a head teacher who was dragged to his death for more than a mile while trapped under the wheels of a car.

Simon Richardson crashed into 56-year-old Michael Mullins, who was cycling home from his job at Stretford Grammar School on the evening of 20 April in the village of Warburton in Trafford, Greater Manchester.

Prosecutors claimed Richardson, 35, fled the scene of the crash before stopping to try to dislodge the injured but still-living cyclist and then driving on with Mr Mullins still lodged underneath the vehicle.

Richardson was also convicted of dangerous driving and will return to Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court to be sentenced on Monday.

There were shouts of "Yes!" from the court's public gallery as the murder verdict was returned.

The judge, Mrs Justice Brunner KC, told Richardson that there was only one sentence for murder, namely life imprisonment.

The court heard Richardson had driven through "give way" markings at a junction in Warburton before colliding with the father-of-two, who went under the Volvo XC90.

Richardson then drove off before stopping in a country lane and twice getting out of the vehicle in attempts to pull Mr Mullins free, the jury was told.

He then mounted the grass verge in his Volvo and finally dislodged him before reversing over Mr Mullins, causing "crushing" chest injuries.

Richardson's cousin Gabrielle Debotte, who was a passenger in the front seat of the car, previously told the court that both of them had heard "moaning" shortly after the collision in Paddock Lane and that he had gone on to say: "He is under the car."

The prosecution claimed Mr Mullins' injuries were caused by "dragging and crushing" rather than the impact of the crash itself.

Prosecutor Phil Barnes KC told jurors: "Simon Richardson knew he was there and he inevitably knew what the consequences of driving on would be, and he did it anyway.

"For a split second after the collision, for a brief moment he possibly thought about doing the right thing and getting out and taking ownership of what he had just done and help the man he had just run down.

"But Simon Richardson did not get out. He did not do the right thing. He chose to drive away.

"The obvious reason is because he wanted to escape the consequences of what he had just done."

A motorcyclist followed a trail of blood and discovered Mr Mullins alone and barely breathing as he lay on a grass verge in a secluded country lane in Lymm, Cheshire.

The head teacher was pronounced dead at the scene shortly afterwards by emergency services.

Richardson was arrested the next day following a police chase.

He denied murder as he claimed he did not realise Mr Mullins was underneath his car and said he did not get out of his vehicle in a bid to free him.

But jurors did not believe him and he was found guilty of murder.

Mrs Justice Brunner KC thanked them and acknowledged their job "cannot have been easy".

She discharged the jurors from taking jury service again for 10 years and told them: "This was, I know, an upsetting case and there was evidence which you may have found distressing."

Paying tribute, Mr Mullins's family said: "He was devoted to his family and our lives will never be the same.

"A gap has been left in our hearts and within his role as a head teacher of Stretford Grammar School."

articles.title: 'Collision at 160-200kmph, track pierced bogey': Chilling details from Spain crash that killed 69
articles.summary: Spain’s deadly train collision, which killed 69 people and injured more than 200, occurred after a failure in the railway signalling system forced trains
articles.body: Spain’s deadly train collision, which killed 69 people and injured more than 200, occurred after a failure in the railway signalling system forced trains to switch to a degraded operating mode, with the two trains travelling on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line at different speeds. Initial findings by independent investigators have revealed that the Renfe train was travelling at an estimated 160-200 kmph when it slammed into the stationary Iryo train.The collision occurred at 8.53am on Wednesday at the entrance to Urda station in Toledo province. According to the investigation-opening notice published by Spain’s Independent Administrative Authority for the Technical Investigation of Railway, Maritime and Civil Aviation Accidents and Incidents (AITAT), the eight-carriage Iryo train, travelling from Madrid to Seville with 147 passengers and five crew members, was stationary near a signal when it was struck from behind by an eight-carriage Renfe AVE train carrying 379 passengers and seven crew members.The impact caused the leading carriage of the Renfe train to become embedded in the rear carriage of the Iryo train. Both carriages overturned and ended up at the foot of the railway embankment. The remaining six carriages of the Renfe train stayed on the track bed, while another fell down the embankment. Several carriages of the Iryo train also derailed, with three falling down the embankment.AITAT said the collision speed was estimated at between 160 and 200 kmph, although the precise figure would only be established after extracting data from the trains' onboard event recorders.The preliminary investigation has also pointed to a failure of the LZB signalling system, which began at around 8.31am and forced trains to operate under the alternative Lateral Signalling Block (BSL) system."To manage this situation, the CRC and the train drivers had to exchange a series of information and instructions through formal railway telephone messages," the report said, referring to communications between the control centre and train drivers.It added that the "sequence of failures, instructions and subsequent actions may ultimately have led to the collision, without the necessary protective barriers having intervened to mitigate the situation".However, investigators cautioned against drawing conclusions about the cause of the disaster, saying all possible explanations remained open at this stage. They said the investigation would examine the LZB malfunction, along with environmental, organisational and procedural factors that may have contributed to the accident.The findings come amid growing questions over railway safety and staffing conditions in Spain. Transport Minister Óscar Puente has criticised the decision to allow the Renfe train to resume normal operations while the Iryo train remained stationary. Railway unions, however, have blamed repeated signalling failures and inadequate staffing, arguing that human operators are increasingly being left to manage situations that automated safety systems should handle.The crash was the second major collision on the Madrid-Seville line this year. An earlier accident in January killed 46 people. AITAT said it had begun collecting evidence, documents and data from recording systems. Its final investigation report is expected within a year.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
